items.new: One often hears of writers that rise and swell with their subject, though it may seem an ordinary one. How, then, with me, writing of this Leviathan? Unconsciously my handwriting expands into billboard capitals. Give me a condor's quill! Give me Vesuvius' crater for an inkstand! Friends, hold my arms! For in the mere act of putting pen to my thoughts of this Leviathan, they weary me and make me faint with the outreaching, all-embracing breadth of their sweep, as if to include the whole circle of the sciences, and all the generations of whales and men and mastodons, past, present, and to come, with all the revolving panoramas of empire on earth and throughout the whole universe, not excluding its suburbs. Such, and so magnifying, is the virtue of a large and liberal theme! We expand to its bulk. To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and enduring volume can ever be written on the flea, though many have tried it.

items.new: Before taking up the subject of fossil whales, I present my credentials as a geologist by stating that in my odd moments I have been a stonemason, and also a great digger of ditches, canals and wells, wine-vaults, cellars, and cisterns of all sorts. Likewise, by way of preliminary, I want to remind the reader that while in the earlier geological strata are found the fossils of monsters now almost completely extinct, the later relics discovered in what are called the Tertiary formations seem to be connecting links, or at any rate intervening links, between those creatures from before recorded time and the ones whose remote descendants are said to have entered the Ark. All the fossil whales discovered so far belong to the Tertiary period, which is the last one before the surface formations. And though none of them exactly matches any known species of the present time, they are still similar enough to them in general respects to justify their being ranked as Cetacean fossils.

items.new: Unwittingly here a secret has been divulged which perhaps might more properly have been disclosed before, in due order. Along with many other particulars concerning Ahab, it had always remained a mystery to some why, for a certain period both before and after the sailing of the Pequod, he had hidden himself away with such grand-lama-like seclusion, and for that one interval sought speechless refuge, as it were, among the marble senate of the dead. Captain Peleg's rumored reason for this seemed by no means adequate, though indeed, as touching all Ahab's deeper nature, every revelation partook more of significant darkness than of explanatory light. But in the end it all came out — this one matter did, at least. That dreadful mishap was at the bottom of his temporary seclusion. And not only this, but to that ever-shrinking, dwindling circle ashore who, for any reason, possessed the privilege of a less prohibited approach to him — to that timid circle the above-hinted accident, remaining as it did moodily unexplained by Ahab, invested itself with terrors not entirely unrelated to the land of spirits and of wails. So that, through their concern for him, they had all conspired, so far as they could, to hush up the knowledge of this thing from others. And hence it was that not till a considerable time had passed did it come to light upon the Pequod's decks.
